title: Neuroanatomy, Falx Cerebri -- Introduction
content: The falx cerebri is a structure formed by invagination of the dura mater into the longitudinal fissure between the cerebral hemispheres (see Image . Midline Sagittal Anatomy of the Cranial Dura and Venous Sinuses). This midline dural reflection is a vertical, sickle-shaped fold within the longitudinal fissure that extends from the crista galli, arches superiorly above the corpus callosum, and terminates at the falcotentorial junction on the superior surface of the tentorial cerebelli. The falx cerebri is anchored anteriorly to the crista galli and posteriorly to the internal occipital protuberance, forming a sail-like partition between the cerebral hemispheres, with a free inferior margin positioned just superior to the corpus callosum.

title: Neuroanatomy, Falx Cerebri -- Introduction
content: The falx cerebri has substantial medical significance as a site of neoplasms, traumatic deformation, ossification, and herniation syndromes, with implications for neuroinflammation and intracranial biomechanics. [1] Surgical relevance arises from the relationship of the falx cerebri to the superior and inferior sagittal sinuses, its role as a rigid midline landmark during interhemispheric approaches, and its influence on brain shift and intraoperative navigation accuracy (see Images . Falx Cerebri on Computed Tomography, Coronal View; Falx Cerebri on Computed Tomography, Axial View). Detailed knowledge of falcine structure, attachments, vascular contents, and mechanical properties supports accurate diagnosis, surgical planning, and risk mitigation in neurosurgical and neurotrauma settings.

title: Neuroanatomy, Falx Cerebri -- Structure and Function
content: The brain is enveloped by 3 membranes: pia mater, arachnoid mater, and dura mater. These membranes are collectively termed the "meninges," derived from the Greek word meninx , meaning “membrane.” Historically, Galen described 2 meningeal layers as pacheia and lepte . Al-Majusi, a Persian physician, referred to these layers as the “hard mother” and “thin mother,” considering them the origin of all membranes in the body. Stephan of Antioch later advocated the terms “dura mater” and “pia mater” for the same structures.

title: Neuroanatomy, Falx Cerebri -- Structure and Function
content: The dura mater is a dense, fibrous outer membrane that provides dual-layered protection within the cranial cavity. [2] [3] Within the neurocranium, the dura mater consists of a periosteal layer, which adheres directly to the inner surface of the skull, and a meningeal layer, which envelops the brain in conjunction with the arachnoid and pia mater. The meningeal dura mater invaginates between brain regions to form dural reflections, including the falx cerebri, falx cerebelli, tentorium cerebelli, and sellar diaphragm (see Image . Sagittal View of Cranial Nerves, Dural Membranes, and Venous Sinuses). The falx cerebri separates the cerebral hemispheres and forms channels, termed "dural venous sinuses," that drain cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and blood. [4] The falx cerebri has a sail-like configuration and is anchored anteriorly to the crista galli above the ethmoid bone, posteriorly to the internal occipital protuberance, and superiorly to the periosteal dura mater.

title: Neuroanatomy, Falx Cerebri -- Structure and Function
content: The superior and inferior sagittal sinuses arise from spaces between folds of the meningeal dura mater that constitute the falx cerebri. The superior sagittal sinus courses along the superior margin of the falx cerebri, whereas the inferior sagittal sinus follows the free inferior margin positioned above the corpus callosum (see Image . Superior Sagittal Sinus and Associated Venous Structures). These venous channels receive CSF from arachnoid granulations and venous blood from meningeal and bridging veins draining the dura mater and cerebral parenchyma. [5] Venous outflow from the superior and inferior sagittal sinuses ultimately enters the internal jugular veins and proceeds into the systemic circulation.

title: Neuroanatomy, Falx Cerebri -- Embryology
content: The 3 meningeal layers derive from the meninx primitiva, which consists of meningeal mesenchyme. [6] The arachnoid and pia mater develop from the leptomenix, whereas the dura mater arises from the pachymeninx. The pia and arachnoid mater originate from neural crest cells. The dura mater develops from mesoderm.

title: Neuroanatomy, Falx Cerebri -- Embryology
content: The dura mater forms a single protective layer around the developing spinal cord and a double layer around the skull, ultimately giving rise to the periosteal and meningeal dural membranes. This process parallels the formation of parietal and visceral layers of the peritoneum within the abdominal cavity. The dura mater forms a continuous membrane that folds upon itself, creating a double-layered structure in which the thicker peripheral layer becomes the periosteal dura, and the thinner layer becomes the meningeal dura.

title: Neuroanatomy, Falx Cerebri -- Embryology
content: During brain development, the meningeal dural layer invaginates between brain regions to form dural partitions. Interruptions in cerebral development, such as semilobar holoprosencephaly, can impede the proper formation of these dural partitions. [7] [8] The falx cerebri develops from interhemispheric mesenchyme between 8 and 11 weeks of gestation. During this period, the sagittal plexus of veins differentiates into the superior sagittal sinus. By 11 weeks of gestation, the falx cerebri envelops the sinus within its superior reflections in the interhemispheric fissure. Connexin, a subset of gap junction proteins, plays a pivotal role in intercellular communication during meningeal development. [9]

title: Neuroanatomy, Falx Cerebri -- Blood Supply and Lymphatics
content: The falx cerebri receives its blood supply primarily from 2 vessels. The anterior portion is supplied by the anterior meningeal artery, also termed the "anterior falx artery" or "anterior falcine artery," which arises from the anterior ethmoidal artery. [10] The posterior portion is supplied by the posterior meningeal artery, a branch of the ascending pharyngeal artery. [11]

title: Neuroanatomy, Falx Cerebri -- Blood Supply and Lymphatics
content: Lymphatic drainage of the falx cerebri occurs via meningeal lymphatic vessels that run parallel to the dural sinuses. These vessels drain predominantly along pathways corresponding to the dural sinuses, eventually exiting through the jugular foramen and emptying into the deep cervical lymph nodes. [12] A minority of lymph drains anteriorly through the cribriform plate into the lymphatics of the nasal mucosa.

title: Neuroanatomy, Falx Cerebri -- Blood Supply and Lymphatics
content: Meningeal lymphatics differ from systemic lymphatics in several respects. These vessels mostly lack valves, which in systemic vessels prevent retrograde flow in the low-pressure lymphatic system. Meningeal lymphatics are thinner, follow venous drainage closely, and contain few branch points. [13]

title: Neuroanatomy, Falx Cerebri -- Nerves
content: The falx cerebri receives innervation from all 3 branches of the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V) and sympathetic fibers predominantly from the superior cervical ganglia. [14] The anterior aspect is primarily supplied by anterior meningeal branches of the ethmoidal nerves, originating from the nasociliary nerve of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V1). The posterior 1/3 is innervated by the nervus tentorii of Arnold, a recurrent meningeal branch of cranial nerve V1. [15] Additional contributions may arise from the dorsal rami of cervical nerves 1, 2, and 3, the hypoglossal nerve (cranial nerve XII), and recurrent branches of the vagus nerve (cranial nerve X). [16]

title: Neuroanatomy, Falx Cerebri -- Muscles
content: No muscles attach to or lie within the falx cerebri. The only muscle cells associated with the meninges are smooth muscle cells of the vasculature, which course within the dural layers.

title: Neuroanatomy, Falx Cerebri -- Physiologic Variants
content: The classification system proposed by Jiang and Jia categorizes the falx cerebri into 3 types based on the interspace between its free inferior margin and the superior aspect of the corpus callosum. Type I is characterized by a substantial interspace, whereas Type III exhibits minimal or absent interspace. [17] The interspace is greatest at the anterior aspect of the falx and gradually decreases toward the posterior aspect. A study reported gaps of 14.1/12.4/2.1 mm in the anterior, middle, and posterior portions of the type I variant, compared with 2.3/1.8/0.6 mm in the type III variant. [18]

title: Neuroanatomy, Falx Cerebri -- Physiologic Variants
content: Developmental variants of the falx cerebri include fenestration, hypoplasia, partial agenesis, and, more rarely, total agenesis. Agenesis most frequently occurs in association with Chiari II malformation and other midline developmental anomalies, such as holoprosencephaly. [19] Isolated falx cerebri variations without superior sagittal sinus involvement arise from the close embryological proximity of these structures. Persistent falcine sinuses occur in cases in which the straight sinus fails to develop or becomes thrombosed during development. [20]

title: Neuroanatomy, Falx Cerebri -- Surgical Considerations
content: The falx cerebri serves as a critical midline surgical landmark for neurosurgeons performing interhemispheric transcallosal approaches to the lateral ventricles. The anterior falx has also been employed in magnetic resonance imaging–based estimation of the craniofacial midline. [21] Intraoperative misregistration due to brain shift is a major challenge for navigation. Coregistered B-mode ultrasonography can improve registration accuracy and support surgical planning, as the falx cerebri dampens deformation of adjacent neural tissue. [22] [23] The falx cerebri provides clinical utility during transdural approaches by protecting neurovascular structures in the vicinity of dural reflections, given its containment of the superior and inferior sagittal sinuses. Simulation studies and 3-dimensional reconstructions of the virtual dura mater may facilitate the learning curve for neurosurgical residency training. [24]

title: Neuroanatomy, Falx Cerebri -- Surgical Considerations
content: Penfield and McNaughton first reported asystole following bilateral stimulation of the falx cerebri. The posterior falx, tentorium cerebelli, and dura mater along the middle cranial fossa floor are heavily innervated, and surgical manipulation of these regions can induce sudden bradycardia via the trigeminocardiac reflex. [25] The dorsal tract of the trigeminal nerve within the trigeminal ganglion is the most sensitive region. Branches of the vagus nerve in proximity to this tract may further predispose to sudden bradycardia and asystole under increased vagal tone.

title: Neuroanatomy, Falx Cerebri -- Surgical Considerations
content: Agenesis or partial agenesis of the falx cerebri permits adherence of the cerebral hemispheres and obstructs the midline transcallosal surgical corridor to the ventricles. [26] Complete absence of the falx may create a clinical dilemma and increase the risk of misdiagnosis, as subdural hematomas can cross the midline into the contralateral hemisphere. Fenestrated falx cerebri may mimic traumatic falx defects. Additional sinuses within the tentorium cerebelli can complicate surgical procedures in the falcotentorial region. [27]

title: Neuroanatomy, Falx Cerebri -- Clinical Significance
content: Dural layers and folds serve as natural protective barriers against infection, malignant cells, and the pathogenesis of neurotrauma. The dura mater contributes significantly to neuroinflammation, mediated by matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), particularly MMP-9. [28] Calvarial bone marrow–dura mater channels are postulated to play a critical role in neuroimmune regulation and CSF transport. [29] [30] [31]

title: Neuroanatomy, Falx Cerebri -- Clinical Significance
content: The falx cerebri is a common site of falcine and parasagittal meningiomas, which account for approximately 8.5% of intracranial meningiomas. These tumors are typically benign and form well-circumscribed, usually round masses attached to the dura. Meningiomas primarily arise from arachnoidal cap cells and can provoke seizures. [32] Headaches, nausea, and vomiting are frequent manifestations of increased intracranial pressure following significant tumor growth.

title: Neuroanatomy, Falx Cerebri -- Clinical Significance
content: Biopsy findings reveal tumor cells according to tumor grade and syncytial nests, which may calcify into psammoma bodies. [33] [34] Symptomatic meningiomas are often surgically excised, with occasional preoperative embolization to reduce tumor volume and intraoperative bleeding. Surgical management follows the principles of adequate exposure, devascularization, intracapsular decompression, and complete excision. The main intraoperative concern is damage to the sagittal sinus, which can result in bleeding, air embolism, and malignant brain edema secondary to venous infarction. [35]

title: Neuroanatomy, Falx Cerebri -- Clinical Significance
content: Assessment of sinus patency, potential tumor invasion, and collateral vessel status is essential for formulating a management plan, particularly for tumors located in the middle and posterior thirds of the superior sagittal sinus. More than 50% of falx and parasagittal meningiomas demonstrate a healthy-side predominant tumor vessel ratio. Results from a study reported the middle meningeal artery as the primary tumor-feeding vessel in the anterior and middle regions (72%), whereas extracranial arteries predominated in the posterior region (54%). In contrast, skull base meningiomas received the majority of their blood supply from the internal carotid artery (48%).

title: Neuroanatomy, Falx Cerebri -- Clinical Significance
content: Primary benign cartilaginous tumors of the dura are rare but may develop within the falx cerebri. Intracranial chondroma can arise from ectopic chondrocytes, chondroid metaplasia of meningeal fibroblasts, or perivascular mesenchymal cells following trauma or inflammation. [36] [37] Traumatic brain injury is another common clinical scenario, potentially resulting in a substantial anterior cranial fossa extradural hematoma or frontal contusions. These lesions can produce a significant mass effect, displacing the ipsilateral cingulate gyrus beneath the falx cerebri and causing subfalcine herniation. [38] This phenomenon is most pronounced at the anterior aspect of the falx, where the interspace between its lower margin and the superior aspect of the corpus callosum is greatest. [39]

title: Neuroanatomy, Falx Cerebri -- Clinical Significance
content: Brain deformation model studies demonstrate that lateral impacts correlate with displacement of the falx cerebri and trauma to the corpus callosum in sports-related concussions, with the rigid falx amplifying strains within the corpus callosum. [40] [41] Mechanical stiffness also differs between dural folds and the underlying venous sinuses, influencing stress distribution during intracranial loading. [42] Falx ossification, reported in 3% of cases, is predominantly benign. [43]

title: Neuroanatomy, Falx Cerebri -- Clinical Significance
content: Ossification may be associated with Gorlin-Goltz syndrome, endocrinopathies, and basal cell nevus syndrome. The falx undergoes ossification because it derives from multipotent mesenchymal cells that can undergo osteogenic differentiation, most commonly following trauma, irritation, or hemorrhage. [44] Ossification increases falcine stiffness, reducing compliance and predisposing to early subfalcine herniation. Artificial intelligence–assisted segmentation of ossified falx has been demonstrated using cone-beam computed tomography.

title: Neuroanatomy, Falx Cerebri -- Other Issues
content: A preserved parasagittal space on coronal computed tomography serves as a reliable radiological indicator for diagnosing spontaneous intracranial hypotension as the underlying cause of chronic subdural hematoma. [45] Physical therapy targeting autonomic regulation and dura mater function has been recently advocated for the management of postcraniotomy headaches. [46]
